title: AI Change Impact and Stakeholder Analysis

questions.question: What is often missing from AI rollout plans?
options: Extra tool screenshots and feature demos, which rollout plans already cover heavily
A rollout plan kept hidden from affected teams until adoption has already been measured
Role-specific impact, stakeholder planning, communication, and manager enablement
Nothing beyond tool access and one training session, which cover adoption on their own
questions.explanation: AI rollouts usually focus on tools and training; what goes missing is role impact, stakeholder needs, communication, and manager enablement — not more screenshots, a concealed plan, or the assumption that tool access alone drives adoption.

questions.question: A new AI assistant goes live, but team leads say they cannot explain to their people what is now expected of them day to day. Which of the lesson's four signals does this match most directly?
options: Role impact — the tasks a specific role performs are changing because of the rollout
Manager dependency — adoption stalls because leads cannot brief their teams on expectations
Communication gap — affected people never received a message explaining the change at all, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
Adoption risk — the change is likely to stall even though the tool itself works fine
questions.explanation: Team leads who cannot explain the new expectations is the lesson's manager-dependency signal, answered with a manager brief — distinct from role impact (the tasks themselves changing), a communication gap (no message sent), or general adoption risk.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A finished organisation chart showing every role after the AI rollout is complete
A deployed AI assistant that is already live for all of the affected teams
A training certificate confirming each affected employee completed onboarding
A ranked change-impact plan mapping signals to stakeholder and manager controls
questions.explanation: The artifact ranks rollout scenarios and maps signals such as adoption risk to controls like impact map, stakeholder plan, communication script, and manager brief — it does not produce an org chart, deploy the assistant, or certify training.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: Manager brief — material that lets leads explain the change and the new expectations
Skipping the communication script so each team improvises its own rollout message, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
Hiding the role-impact analysis so affected staff do not worry before the launch
Dropping the stakeholder plan because training attendance already proves adoption
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls are impact map, stakeholder plan, communication script, and manager brief — a manager brief gives leads the material to explain the change, unlike skipping the script, hiding role impact, or dropping the stakeholder plan.

questions.question: When does an AI rollout need a formal change plan?
options: When people impact, adoption complexity, role impact, or manager dependency is high
Only when no role's daily work changes as a result of introducing the AI tool
Only after adoption has already failed and teams have returned to the old process — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
Never — one training session covers everything an AI rollout plan needs to cover
questions.explanation: High people impact, adoption complexity, role impact, or manager dependency are exactly the signals that call for structured change planning — not the absence of role changes, a post-mortem after adoption failed, or training on its own.

questions.question: What should stakeholder planning clarify?
options: Only which vendor supplies the AI tool being introduced across the affected teams
Only the launch date, since the rest of the rollout can be worked out afterwards
Nothing about who owns communication, since each affected team will sort that out
Who is affected, what changes, what message they need, and who reinforces it
questions.explanation: Stakeholder planning is specific about who is affected, what changes for them, the message they need, and who reinforces it — not just the vendor, the launch date, or an unowned communication effort.
